nameStory: The Great Crested Flycatcher gets its name from the prominent feathered crest on the back of its head, which it can raise and lower like a mohawk hairstyle. The "great" part distinguishes it from smaller crested flycatchers, while "flycatcher" describes its hunting method of darting out from perches to snatch insects right out of the air. It's like having a built-in insect radar system with a punk rock hairdo!
description: The Great Crested Flycatcher is a large, robust songbird about the size of a robin that specializes in catching flying insects. It has a brownish-olive back, a grayish throat and chest, and a bright yellow belly that really pops when you see it. The most distinctive feature is its shaggy crest of feathers on the back of its head, giving it a perpetually "bed head" appearance. These birds are the largest flycatchers you're likely to see in New England's forests.

idTips.label: Prominent crest
idTips.description: A distinctive tuft of feathers on the back of the head that can be raised or lowered, creating a shaggy, unkempt appearance that's visible even from a distance

idTips.label: Bright yellow belly
idTips.description: The lower chest and belly are a vibrant lemon-yellow color that contrasts sharply with the duller upper parts, especially noticeable when the bird is perched

idTips.label: Rusty tail feathers
idTips.description: The tail shows distinctive reddish-brown or rusty colored outer feathers that flash when the bird flies, creating a warm cinnamon accent

idTips.label: Large size and thick bill
idTips.description: Noticeably larger than most other flycatchers with a broad, flat bill perfect for snapping up insects, giving it a robust, sturdy appearance

idTips.label: Loud wheep call
idTips.description: A distinctive ascending whistle that sounds like "wheep!" or "preet!" - sharp, clear, and carrying well through the forest canopy

habitat: Great Crested Flycatchers prefer mature deciduous and mixed forests with large trees and open understories, especially areas with oak, maple, and hickory trees. They're most common in woodland edges, parks, and suburban areas with tall shade trees, typically staying high in the canopy 20-60 feet off the ground. You'll rarely see them in dense, young forests or completely open areas without substantial tree cover.

seasonality.spring: Arrives in late April to early May with males establishing territories through loud calling. This is the best time to hear their distinctive wheep calls echoing through the awakening forest as they compete for nesting sites in tree cavities.
seasonality.summer: Most active and visible during breeding season, frequently seen darting out from high perches to catch insects. Parents become busy feeding young in tree holes, making multiple trips with beaks full of bugs.
seasonality.fall: Becomes quieter and less conspicuous in late August through September as they prepare for migration. Still present but spending more time silently foraging before departing for warmer climates.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent from New England, having migrated to Central and South America. Any flycatcher-like bird seen in winter would be a different species entirely.

funFact: Great Crested Flycatchers are obsessed with decorating their tree cavity nests with shed snakeskins - and if they can't find real ones, they'll use clear plastic wrap, cellophane, or even onion skins as substitutes, creating what looks like the world's strangest bird interior design project!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Eastern Kingbirds, but remember "Yellow belly, crested crown = Great Crested Flycatcher; White belly, flat crown = Eastern Kingbird." The crest is usually the dead giveaway - if you see that messy feather tuft on the head, you've found your Great Crested Flycatcher.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "tyrant" flycatchers (referring to their aggressive insect-hunting behavior), Great Crested Flycatchers are actually quite gentle with other bird species and focus their tyrannical tendencies exclusively on flying insects. The family name comes from their domineering attitude toward their prey, not toward other birds.
compareHints: The Great Crested Flycatcher is the only member of the Myiarchus genus regularly found in New England, making it unique among its close relatives here. Compared to other large flycatchers like the Eastern Kingbird, it's much more yellow below and has that distinctive crest, plus it prefers forest canopies rather than open perches. Its size and crest make it unmistakable among New England's flycatcher family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the great crested flycatcher, the ash-throated flycatcher is smaller and much more subtly colored.
